overview: Ampelosaurus atacis was a titanosaurian sauropod from the Late Cretaceous of southern France and Spain, living approximately 71–66 million years ago. Estimated at about 15 metres in length, it is known from teeth, postcranial bones, and notably osteoderms — bony dermal armour — preserved in the Marnes Rouges Inférieures Formation of the Aude region. It inhabited the coastal lowlands of the Ibero-Armorican island landmass during the final stages of the Cretaceous.

Named by Le Loeuff in 1995, Ampelosaurus is classified within Lirainosaurinae, a group of European titanosaurs. The presence of osteoderms in an otherwise modestly-sized titanosaur makes it a valuable taxon for studying the evolution of armour in sauropods. It is one of the best-known European Late Cretaceous sauropods, with material recovered from multiple sites in France and Spain.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Ampelosaurus atacis was named by Jean Le Loeuff in 1995 based on material collected from the Marnes Rouges Inférieures Formation in the Aude department of southern France. The generic name derives from Greek ampelos (vineyard) and sauros (lizard), reflecting the vineyard-covered landscape of the discovery region. The species name refers to the Atax River (modern Aude).

articles.title: Anatomy and Osteoderms
articles.body: Ampelosaurus is distinguished from many other European titanosaurs by the preservation of bony osteoderms, which formed a dermal armour over parts of the body. These structures vary in shape and size and were embedded in the skin rather than attached to the skeleton. Vertebrae and limb elements show the typical lightweight, air-sac-filled construction of titanosaurs.

articles.title: Ecology and Palaeoenvironment
articles.body: Ampelosaurus inhabited the Ibero-Armorican island, a landmass formed in southwestern Europe during the Late Cretaceous as the Tethys Sea encroached. This insularity may have influenced the body size and diversity of the dinosaur fauna, a phenomenon known as insular dwarfism seen in other European titanosaurs such as Magyarosaurus.

articles.title: Significance
articles.body: As one of the most completely known Late Cretaceous sauropods from Europe, Ampelosaurus is a key reference for understanding titanosaur diversity on the European archipelago. Its osteoderm-bearing integument adds to evidence that armour evolved independently multiple times within Titanosauria, offering insights into the functional and ecological pressures shaping sauropod anatomy.

record.mya: early Maastrichtian, about 71.5 million years ago
record.description: Ampelosaurus atacis was an early Maastrichtian titanosaur from the Bellevue bonebed in southern France. The holotype is three connected dorsal vertebrae, while abundant referred material includes other vertebrae, girdle and limb bones, teeth and several forms of osteoderm. The bonebed contains multiple individuals, but not every titanosaur bone from Bellevue can automatically be assigned to Ampelosaurus.
facts: The holotype MDE C3-247 consists of three connected middle dorsal vertebrae from the Bellevue locality.
The original diagnosis also drew on abundant disarticulated postcranial bones and plate-, bulb- and spine-shaped osteoderms.
The site preserves many individuals rather than one complete skeleton; later work has cautioned that more than one titanosaur morphotype may be present.
Bone histology shows prolonged growth and extensive remodelling, while exact adult size estimates remain dependent on associating isolated limb bones correctly.
Ampelosaurus is usually recovered among European lithostrotian titanosaurs, commonly within Lirainosaurinae.

animalParagraphs: Ampelosaurus was a medium-sized titanosaur that lived in southern France around 71 million years ago, when much of Europe was an archipelago of islands. It had the classic sauropod build of a long neck and tail, a deep body and pillar-like legs, and its skin was studded with bony osteoderms of several shapes.

It is known from the Bellevue bonebed near Campagne-sur-Aude, where hundreds of bones from many individuals accumulated. Vertebrae, girdle bones, limb bones, teeth and osteoderms are all represented, and cranial material including a braincase has been attributed to the genus.

The wealth of material makes Ampelosaurus one of the best-sampled European titanosaurs, but the bones are disarticulated and may not all belong to one species. Bone histology shows slow, prolonged growth, and mature size remains an estimate that depends on which isolated limb bones are associated together.
animalHighlights: Hundreds of bones from the Bellevue bonebed document most regions of the skeleton.
Plate-, bulb- and spine-shaped osteoderms show that the skin carried bony armour of more than one form.
Bone microstructure records slow, extended growth compared with many other sauropods.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by teeth and body plan
lifeCards.reason: Slender, peg-like teeth and the long neck fit a browsing herbivore. The specific plants eaten are not preserved.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Robust, columnar limb bones show habitual four-legged walking.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: No single individual is complete, so length is reconstructed from separately found limb and vertebral elements.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Osteoderm shapes are known, but none has been found in place on the body, so their layout is reconstructed.

presentation.classificationSummary: Ampelosaurus is a lithostrotian titanosaur, usually placed among the European forms grouped as Lirainosaurinae. Its exact relationships within Lithostrotia vary among analyses.

questions.title: Is there more than one titanosaur at Bellevue?
questions.copy: Later studies have suggested that the bonebed may contain a second morphotype, so not every bone can be assumed to be Ampelosaurus.

questions.title: Which bones belonged together?
questions.copy: The bones are disarticulated and come from many individuals. Reconstructing one animal means associating elements that were not found connected.

questions.title: How were the osteoderms arranged?
questions.copy: Several osteoderm shapes are known, but their positions on the body have not been observed and remain reconstructed.

review.ageReviewNote: The headline age is restricted to the early Maastrichtian Bellevue type locality. Wider French and Spanish referrals need specimen-level taxonomic review and should not silently extend the range of the genus.

evidence.summary: A multi-individual bonebed preserves abundant titanosaur material and several osteoderm forms, but it is not one complete skeleton and may include more than one morphotype.
evidence.material: Holotype of three connected dorsal vertebrae plus abundant disarticulated vertebral, girdle, limb, dental and osteoderm material.
evidence.formations: Bellevue locality, Upper Aude Valley, southern France.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Many body regions are represented, while specimen association, maximum size and assignment of every bone to Ampelosaurus remain uncertain.
evidence.sourceBasis: Le Loeuff 1995, Klein et al. 2012 and Fondevilla et al. 2016.

panel.headline: Three joined vertebrae name the species; a bonebed of many animals fills in the rest.
panel.standfirst: Ampelosaurus is anchored by three articulated dorsal vertebrae from Bellevue. The same bonebed has yielded hundreds of disarticulated bones, teeth and osteoderms from multiple individuals, which together document most of the skeleton without preserving any single complete animal.

coverage.label: Moderate
coverage.basis: Most skeletal regions are represented across the bonebed, but the material is disarticulated, comes from many individuals and may include a second titanosaur.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Vertebrae from the neck, back and tail, girdle and limb bones, teeth, cranial elements including a braincase, and osteoderms of plate, bulb and spine form, all recovered from the Bellevue bonebed.
knownRemains.note: Because the bones were not found in association, assigning every element to Ampelosaurus, and to a particular individual, depends on interpretation rather than direct observation.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Isolated teeth and cranial elements including a braincase attributed to the genus; no complete skull.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Holotype dorsal series plus numerous cervical, dorsal and caudal vertebrae, ribs and chevrons from other individuals.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Scapulae, pelvic bones, humeri, femora and other limb elements; hand and foot bones are less well represented.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Osteoderms of several shapes and sampled bone histology; no skin impressions, colour or gut contents are known.

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: A holotype of three articulated vertebrae and an abundant, disarticulated multi-individual assemblage from the same site.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A mid-sized armoured lithostrotian titanosaur, one of the best-sampled Late Cretaceous sauropods of the European archipelago.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Which bones belong to which individual, whether all belong to one species, maximum adult size, and the arrangement of the osteoderms.
